title: Ingest-to-Inference Catalog Tour & Bench Plan
summary: Quick demo of Redwood's model catalog (API + Console + Optimize) focused on ingest-to-inference workflow. Covered how to pick open models, read compatibility matrices, run bench requests, and plan a small pilot. Customer wants predictable latency at 95th pct and data residency; discussed Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs and next steps for a pilot with a benchmark spreadsheet.
next_steps: Maria: send tailored bench request template and cost breakdown by 2025-11-07
Tomás: schedule kernel-mapping deep-dive (30m) with Priya the week of 11/10
Customer: provide 3 representative prompt sets and typical seq lengths by 2025-11-06
action_items: Maria Lopez - Send pricing + dedicated capacity options by 2025-11-07
Tomás Nguyen - Share kernel mapping notes and initial quantization suggestions by 2025-11-10
Ethan Ross - Upload sample prompt sets and traffic profile to shared repo by 2025-11-06
transcript:
[00:00] Maria Lopez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Today we wanted to run through a focused tour — from ingest to inference — using the catalog, show how we pick open models, read the compatibility matrix, and kick off a bench.
[00:12] Ethan Ross: Great, thanks Maria. We're trying to understand tradeoffs — our SLO is 95th percentile below 120ms for single-turn QA, and our infra is a mix of GCP us-west and an on-prem kubernetes cluster.
[00:24] Tomás Nguyen: Yep, that's helpful, Ethan. We'll highlight Hosted vs Dedicated and the Private options for VPCs. Quick question, Priya, are you constrained by GPU types on-prem?
[00:33] Priya Shah: Yeah, we're primarily A100s but some older T4 nodes in edge racks. We also need KMS for keys — SOC 2 is a requirement.
[00:41] Maria Lopez: Perfect, we'll call that out. Ok open the console — top-left is the model catalog. The catalog has curated open models and breakdowns: tokenization, memory footprint, fp16 vs int8 friendliness, and a hardware compatibility matrix.
[00:58] Jon Meyer: Can you show how you'd pick a model for lower latency but still decent accuracy?
[01:05] Tomás Nguyen: Sure, so we usually filter by task (chat/generation/embedding), then by target sequence length and quantization profiles. For your 120ms SLO we look at sequence lengths first — small context windows tend to allow smaller models or optimized kernels.
[01:22] [01:22] Speaker 1: (muffled) and also prefix caching can help..
[01:25] Maria Lopez: Right — prefix/KV cache is big when you have repeated system prompts. We demoed a bench earlier where prefix caching saved 30% tokens and 20% latency at P95 for a FAQ workload.
[01:40] Ethan Ross: How do you interpret the compatibility matrix? We saw a column for "quant-aware kernels" and one for "cpu fallback".
[01:48] Tomás Nguyen: The matrix maps model families to kernel implementations and hardware rows (A100, H100, T4, CPU). Green means native optimized kernel (fastest), yellow is less optimal but supported, red sometimes means not recommended or out-of-memory risk. There's also a note on sequence length breakpoints — e.g., model X uses fused attention up to 1024 tokens on H100 and falls back to a generic kernel beyond that which increases latency.
[02:14] Priya Shah: That helps. What about quantization? We want to try int8 or LLM.int8 — is that automated?
[02:20] Tomás Nguyen: Optimize in the Console gives sugggested quant profiles per workload. For open models we surface community-verified quant profiles and recommended retrain/ptq recipes. We can recommend int8 for throughput and show expected quality deltas in the bench report.
[02:36] Jon Meyer: Any pointers on routing/fallbacks if capacity is constrained? We can't have high error rates in production.
[02:43] Maria Lopez: We showed routed policies — you can set primary model and a cheaper fallback or smaller context variant. If latency spikes or capacity hits, the smart router will route to fallback automatically and we emit autoplay events to the console so you can see rollback windows.
[02:57] Ethan Ross: Good. Can we run a bench on our prompts? What does that process look like?
[03:02] Tomás Nguyen: Yes. We ask for a sample prompt set and traffic profile (qps, seq lengths). We spin bench runs in Dedicated or Hosted infra depending on preference. For your case, I'd recommend a bench step matrix: one hosted run at our fastest kernels, one dedicated commit simulating burst, and one on-prem validation mapping kernels to your A100s. That gives end-to-end numbers.
[03:25] [03:25] Speaker 2: (clears throat) there's also the cost-per-token calc.
[03:28] Maria Lopez: Exactly, Optimize will show token-level cost and latency breakdowns. We'll attach a cost sheet. For data residency we can do Private deployment in your VPC and integrate with your KMS. That was requested — correct?
[03:40] Priya Shah: Yes, KMS + audit logs + SSO; we use Okta.
[03:45] Tomás Nguyen: We support SAML/Okta provisioning and audit log export. We'll also show a sample SOC 2 artifact in the follow up.
[03:53] Jon Meyer: When you say "bench" — is the bench reproducible by us, or is it Redwood-run only?
[03:58] Maria Lopez: Both. We provide the bench harness and template (the bench request template). You can run it in your lab, or we can run it and give the exact config. For kernel mapping we'll do a short reproducible run on your infra.
[04:10] Ethan Ross: Ok, what's the timeline to get useful numbers?
[04:13] Tomás Nguyen: Once we have samples and traffic profile, a basic bench can be spun up in 3-4 business days; kernel mapping and on-prem validation add another week. So total ~10 business days to a thorough bench report.
[04:26] Priya Shah: Do you also run quantized runs? We need to see quality delta metrics.
[04:30] Tomás Nguyen: Yes, bench report includes quality evaluation (BLEU / exact match / custom scoring you define) alongside latency and cost. We can include an A/B prompt split for regression checks.
[04:43] Maria Lopez: I'm going to walk through a sample bench report in the console — here's the summary page, key tabs: latency, cost, quality, kernel heatmap. The heatmap shows hotspots where attention kernels fallback and latency jumps.
[04:57] [04:57] Speaker 1: oh that heatmap's nice.
[04:59] Tomás Nguyen: We also show sequence-length distributions on the report so you can see where your P95 is coming from.
[05:06] Ethan Ross: Any gotchas for on-prem? We have mixed GPU drivers versions and custom CVM images.
[05:12] Tomás Nguyen: Driver mismatch is the usual culprit. For kernel mapping we need driver and CUDA versions and access to 1 representative node for profiling. We'll provide a small profiling container that runs a few kernels and returns artifacts. That helps us pick the right kernels and fallback settings.
[05:28] Priya Shah: Sounds doable. What's next after bench? Rollout?
[05:31] Maria Lopez: Rollouts are configured in the Console — canary percentages, auto-fallback policies when error rates exceed thresholds, and model pinning. We typically recommend a progressive canary: 1% -> 5% -> 20% over days while watching quality regressions.
[05:45] Jon Meyer: Ok, let's talk pricing briefly — Hosted for quick start vs Dedicated committed capacity.
[05:50] Maria Lopez: Hosted is pay-as-you-go; Dedicated gets you reserved GPU pools with better predictable latency and unit cost. We'll include a cost comparison for your expected qps. Also, Dedicated supports VPC peering and private endpoint.
[06:05] Ethan Ross: Any competitor differences to call out?
[06:08] Tomás Nguyen: A couple: some providers push a single endpoint-only model and limited kernel visibility; Redwood surfaces kernel mapping, per-token cost, and rollout tooling — plus private deployment. Anthropic and OpenAI have higher-level model offerings but less control over kernel/runtime optimizations. Vertex AI has good infra but fewer open-model bench templates.
[06:27] Priya Shah: Good to know.
[06:29] Maria Lopez: Next steps — we'll send the bench request template and pricing. Tomas will schedule kernel mapping call. Anything else?
[06:37] Ethan Ross: Please add a privacy/data flow diagram — legal will ask.
[06:40] Maria Lopez: Will do, we'll attach the architecture diagram and SOC 2 brief.
[06:45] Jon Meyer: Alright thanks — any final notes?
[06:47] Tomás Nguyen: We'll try to keep bench runs reproducible; when you upload prompts please tag the traffic profile.
[06:53] Maria Lopez: Great, I'll follow up with everything by Friday. Thanks everyone.
[06:58] [End of transcript]
